newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish govt body says EMU negative in short term.
newsitem.headline: Swedish govt body says EMU negative in short term.

text.p: A Swedish government probe into the consequences of Swedish participation in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) said on Monday the arguments against a common currency had the upper hand in the short term.

"We don't think that Sweden should join in 1999, because we don't think the economic and political conditions are at hand," professor Harry Flam of the Swedish Government Commission on EMU told Reuters.

Although there were good arguments for the EMU project as such, the Calmfors commission, named after chairman Lars Calmfors, concluded in its final report that membership in 1999 would be premature for Sweden.
"Our overall assessment of economic and political factors is that the arguments against Swedish participation in 1999 are stronger than the arguments in favour of it," the report said.

Charged with examining the consequences of Swedish participation in the monetary union that is due to start on January 1 1999, the eight-strong team of academics said it was impossible to draw unambiguous conclusions.
Even if it were to reject EMU membership, Sweden should leave the door ajar for participation at some later date.
"A possible Swedish decision not to enter in 1999 should be formulated as if we aim to participate later when the conditions are at hand," the commission said.

Although arguments such as social and economic efficiency tended to support Swedish membership, the country's lengthening dole queues called into question the appropriateness of a single currency, Flam said.

"Our prime argument is the unemployment situation. We're not used to having 13 percent total unemployment, and we're very worried that something might happen in the next few years that might increase that level," he said.
But political factors played their part, Flam added.
"There is also a political argument for waiting. The issue is quite new to the Swedish voters, and we think we need time to have a comprehensive and factual discusssion about this issue," he said.

The main alternative to full EMU membership presented in the Calmfors report was the status quo, ruling out participation in the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) as a precursor to joining the single currency.
"The economic arguments speak for maintaining the current monetary policy strategy of a flexible exchange rate and an inflation target," the report said.
"The commission sees substantial risks in participating in an ERM system where economic policy once again may have to be directed towards supporting an exchange rate target."

Although the commission suggested that Swedish participation in the single currency could be a more attractive option further down the road, the report's generally negative tone will fuel the growing opposition to the project.

A majority of Swedes are against the single currency -- and against EU membership as a whole -- and it is doubtful whether Prime Minister Goran Persson could command a parliamentary majority for the single currency in a free vote.

As it is, the decision will effectively be taken by the ruling Social Democratic Party congress in September 1997, when it is likely to be swayed by the opinions of Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink. Both are believed to be supporters of the single currency.
Analysts said that even though the commission had the government's backing, its conclusions were by no means the final word on the matter.

"I think Goran Persson and the government will make up their own minds. This is one element in the debate, but it is not decisive for what the party leadership and the governent decide in the end," Hubert Fromlet of Sweden's Swedbank told Reuters.
